summary: How a RoleCall preset becomes a SillyTavern preset, separating what converts mechanically from the remainder needing human judgment. A RoleCall preset can carry a second program beside its prompts: a hook machine writing variables as text passes through, and conditionals reading them back. The page is one crossing on purpose while the machinery is not, since macros resolve through a canonical operation hub and no engine pair is written down anywhere; these are the judgment calls left after the hub does everything derivable. Converting without a decision: separator differences from each catalog's declared forms, indexed access lowering onto variables whose names carry the index, conditionals preserved rather than flattened because SillyTavern's current engine has them, and macros nested in blocks or passed as arguments. Kit reports facts without deciding them, in a structure section carrying arrays, domains, wideVariables, pushHooks, choices resolved to their declared options, markerCandidates, and stateLayer as read, absent or unknown, where unknown rather than zero prevents absence reading as none. Four patterns follow: a choice group becomes a seeded variable; fix the producer not the consumer for regex; a closed domain expands into a conditional for upper; and a macro becomes a marker prompt, which the converter cannot do because translation never adds, removes or repositions blocks. Hook set actions map onto regex scripts because replacements are macro-substituted after capture groups fill in, but push has no counterpart. Evidence is labeled unit-proven, integration-proven or code-read. Measured on one 9,286-token preset: 86 unsupported macros before, 0 after.
topics: canonical operation hub no pair table

sections.title: What converts without a decision
sections.summary: Handled in code, appearing in the transfer receipt only as rewrite entries. Separator differences resolve because each catalog declares the shape of its own forms, so roll with double-colon becomes roll with single colon without either engine knowing about the other. Indexed access lowers because SillyTavern has no arrays but an array of fixed slots is a set of variables whose names carry the index: getvarkey on propp_plan at 3 becomes getvar on propp_plan_3, and a computed index becomes a composed name, which works because a nested macro resolves before its consumer. SillyTavern documents exactly this shape itself. Conditionals are preserved rather than flattened because SillyTavern's current macro engine has if, else, closing tags, inversion and comparison; the target's own catalog decides this through the canonical flow.conditional operation, and an engine without conditionals still gets blocks flattened to their body with the condition kept as a comment. Macros nested inside a preserved block, or passed as arguments to a portable macro, are translated too; both were defects at one point and both are now covered by tests.

sections.title: What Kit reports
sections.summary: The engine computes facts and does not decide what to do about them. A preset transfer or export receipt carries a structure section: arrays answering which variables are addressed by index, which literal indices appear, and how many accesses use a computed index; domains for variables whose every written value was a short literal, with the value set; wideVariables for variables that are literal but too long or too many to expand inline, named rather than dropped in silence; pushHooks for hooks that append to a list, with the trigger regex verbatim; choices, each choice macro resolved against the choice group it names with that group's declared options and default; markerCandidates for dead macros whose name resembles a canonical marker slot; and stateLayer as read, absent, or unknown. stateLayer deserves attention because a RoleCall hook machine lives only in escrow and never in the canonical body, so a piece whose escrow was dropped reports unknown rather than zero hooks, since zero read as there are none is precisely the mistake this distinction exists to prevent.

sections.title: Pattern 1: a choice group becomes a seeded variable
sections.summary: The choice macro asks RoleCall for the option a user picked at load time, and SillyTavern has no such concept, so the macro is removed on the way out and the receipt records it. The choice group itself survives conversion as canonical data, so the receipt can hand you its options. Replace the read with an ordinary variable and seed that variable once at the top of the preset: a seed block placed first sets the variable to a value, and every former choice read becomes a plain getvar. The seed is the group's declared default when it has one. A person switching options edits one line instead of hunting every reference, which is the closest thing to the original behaviour a preset without a picker can offer.

sections.title: Pattern 2: fix the producer, not the consumer
sections.summary: The regex macro post-processes a value inline, SillyTavern has no such macro, and there is no expression that replaces it in place. The move is to stop needing it: a value that has to be cleaned before use is a value produced wrong, and the producer is almost always reachable, being the hook or the write that built the string, so clean it there once instead of at every read. Where the transformation genuinely belongs at the boundary, SillyTavern regex scripts can carry it. They are not macros and do not appear in the macro catalog, so the converter will not reach for them on your behalf and adding one is a deliberate act.

sections.title: Pattern 3: a closed domain expands into a conditional
sections.summary: The upper macro has no SillyTavern equivalent. Applied to a variable whose values are unknown it is unfixable; applied to one whose value set is closed it is a lookup. This is why the receipt reports domains: when every write is a short literal the full value set is known, so the uppercase form can be written beside the value, after which the upper read becomes a plain getvar. Check the receipt first, because the pattern needs a literal assignment site and only works for a variable listed under domains; in the preset measured here upper was applied to a computed variable, where the fix is Pattern 2. Domains counts every write form, not just setvar: shorthand assignment, addvar, incvar and decvar all open a domain, since a value derived from the current one cannot be enumerated. Three variables there looked like the closed set containing zero until the arithmetic writes driving them were counted; they are counters, and expanding one into a constant would badly mislead.

sections.title: Pattern 4: a macro becomes a marker prompt
sections.summary: The message_history macro splices the transcript. SillyTavern does this too but not with a macro: it uses a marker prompt, a prompt-list entry with the identifier chatHistory that the prompt builder positions during assembly. So the conversion is not a rewrite but a deletion plus a structural edit, removing the macro then enabling or adding a marker block at the position the macro occupied. The converter cannot do this. Translation rewrites text within a block and does not add, remove, or reposition blocks. That is a real boundary and not an oversight, and it is why markerCandidates reports a candidate for a person to act on rather than performing the promotion. The same reasoning covers dialogueExamples, worldInfoBefore, worldInfoAfter, and the other marker slots.

sections.title: The hook machine
sections.summary: RoleCall's macro_engine_yaml is a list of regex-triggered hooks: a trigger, flags, a placement of user_input or ai_output, an optional strip, and actions that set, unset, append or push a variable. The pieces line up with SillyTavern regex scripts more closely than they first appear, since a regex script has a find pattern, a replacement, and a placement whose values include user input and AI output. Crucially a replacement is macro-substituted after capture groups are filled in, so a replacement containing a setvar really does write state, and a hook that sets a variable has a direct counterpart. Push does not: it appends each match to a list and SillyTavern has no lists, so it lowers onto numbered variables, meaning one hook becomes as many captures as the array has slots. The receipt gives both numbers, pushHooks carrying the trigger verbatim and arrays giving the index range the reads use, so the count is measured rather than guessed. Nothing here is automated: Hoplight seals macro_engine_yaml as escrow and never executes it.

sections.title: Evidence
sections.summary: Claims are backed at different strengths and the difference matters. Unit-proven covers separator rewriting, indexed-access lowering, block preservation, nested-argument translation, and every field of the structure report, in translate.test.ts and structure.test.ts. Integration-proven covers a RoleCall preset crossing to SillyTavern through the real adapter registry, resolving its dialect from escrow and carrying structural findings into the receipt, in transfer-e2e.test.ts. Code-read covers SillyTavern's regex replacement path calling substituteParams, its placement values, and its marker prompt identifiers, all read from that project's source; the four patterns themselves are recommendations for an author and not implemented behaviour. Measured on one 9,286-token RoleCall preset: 86 macros unsupported by SillyTavern before translation, 0 after, across 92 rewrites and 4 removals, and the 4 removals are one instance of each pattern.
